prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms held at the magic wavelength brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B037 to B042 with Katori and Ye. The reason is not the count of colleagues who prefer it; it is that the chair's question on B037 has an answer that works against my own first choice. The tunnel magnetoresistance story has three steps: the 1995 room-temperature effect (Miyazaki, Moodera), the symmetry-selective MgO mechanism with its 2004 demonstration of coherent tunnelling (Parkin, and independently Yuasa and Djayaprawira), and the industrial development. A fair citation for the step I value most needs Parkin and Yuasa, and the 1995 step needs Miyazaki and Moodera. That is four or five people for a three-name limit, and I cannot honestly say Yuasa and Djayaprawira should replace one of the supplied three, because the supplied three are the ones who cover the discovery and the industrial realisation. I therefore withdraw B037 as my first choice and keep it as an alternative, since the physics is closed and I still think it is overdue. On B042 I now find the scientific case sufficient. The lattice clock is a distinct principle: the magic-wavelength condition makes the trapping light shift cancel for the clock transition, which allows many neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no Doppler or recoil broadening and a statistical advantage over a single ion. As a theorist of electronic structure I note that reaching 1e-18 depended on calculated and measured atomic properties (blackbody shift, hyperpolarisability, higher-order light shifts), which is the kind of detail that tells me this is a real physical step and not only engineering. Reproduction across Sr, Yb and Hg and several continents is the maturity test and it is passed. The citation should rest on both parts of the chair's question, the magic-wavelength lattice architecture and the demonstrated 1e-18 performance, and should claim nothing about the comb or ion clocks, nuclear clocks or the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objections are priority and overlap. Takamoto and Ido gave the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration and Lemonde's group contributed to the early Sr clock and the cross-checks; none is among the two names, and a two-name prize states a judgement that Katori originated the concept and Ye made it the record-setting standard. Ye's name is also tied to comb and ultrastable-laser work that the 2005 prize touched, so his credit has to be tied to the lattice clock in the text. Pearce's point that the clock refines a measurement capability opened up by 2005 and 2012 is not trivial, and I cannot dismiss it merely because the committee majority leans the other way. I also share Lindroth's warning that agreement among members with an atomic-physics vantage is not evidence of merit. My own vantage is not atomic physics, which is a small point in favour of my reading, but I am moving from a corner I know to one I cannot check against first-hand experience, and I should say so.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the many-atom, light-shift-cancelled lattice is a new principle rather than a refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, that the citation should rest on demonstrated 1e-18 performance and comparisons, and that Ye should be credited strictly for the lattice clock.
responses.response: In round 1 I called the Katori and Ye pairing less clean than he did, and I still think the committee has to choose between a prize for the concept and one for record accuracy. After the exchange I think it can choose both, in one sentence, because Katori's idea and Ye's realisation are separable and are the two parts of the citation. I agree with him that thorium and the redefinition of the second stay out of the text. Where I still differ is that a two-name credit does not remove the Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde problem; it only makes the committee decide it openly. I accept that decision and think Katori's concept and Ye's many-atom realisation to 1e-18 are the decisive steps.

responses.point: Pearce prefers IceCube as a new observational channel and regards the lattice clock as a refinement of a capability created by the 2005 and 2012 prizes, while naming B042 as his first alternative and saying he would be comfortable with it.
responses.response: I take his distinction between a new channel and a refinement seriously, and I answer it with a specific test. The 2005 prize gave a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize gave control of single trapped systems; neither gives a way to interrogate many neutral atoms with the trap perturbation cancelled, and that is what moved accuracy to 1e-18 across laboratories. That is a new principle, not a better ruler. I also share his own reservations about B029 from the files: the diffuse flux is secure but the population origin and the Baikal and DUMAND credit are open. Since he lists B042 as his fallback and I now prefer it, we may not be far apart, and I would ask him to say whether the interpretation of source origin would hold him back from a vote for B029 this year.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B026 on the grounds that nature answered a half-century question, that the 2013 prize covered only theory, and that Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are a defensible leadership proxy, while conceding that the committee should turn elsewhere if no defensible three names exist.
responses.response: I agree the discovery is decisive and I have not discounted it on science. The chair asks whether anyone can state a principle for the three names and say what each did for the 2012 observation. I cannot do that from the supplied evidence, and he does not do it in his file either, so by his own stated rule that the committee should turn elsewhere, B026 has not met the bar for me. I also doubt that discovery of nature should automatically outweigh invention; the prize text names both, and the clock is a discovery in the sense that the lattice cancellation and the 1e-18 systematics were not guaranteed to work. If a majority later accepts the leadership proxy explicitly, I would not call the result unreasonable, but I do not vote for it on the present evidence.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B042 and, in her round-1 reply to me, ranked B037 behind clocks because the Yuasa and Djayaprawira gap affects the main step of the MgO story rather than its edges, while saying the clock gaps (Takamoto, Ido, Lemonde) are at the edges.
responses.response: She was right about this, and it is the distinction that moved me. For B037 the missing names sit at the central step of the physics, whereas for B042 the missing names, though real, are around a concept and a record that two people can be tied to. I would add that her point about Ye's credit resting partly on comb work is the one to settle in the citation wording. I disagree with her only on one thing: waiting for the redefinition of the second is not a reason to hesitate, and I agree with her that the committee should not tie its judgement to a metrological timetable.

responses.point: Johansson asked how I weigh the Yuasa and Djayaprawira contribution against the three supplied B037 names, and has not ranked tunnel magnetoresistance, while also keeping B007 as an alternative because of the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission and the 2016 prize.
responses.response: My answer is that the contribution should not be weighed away: the coherent MgO result of 2004 has two independent groups, and a fair account puts Yuasa alongside Parkin. With a three-name limit that means dropping Miyazaki or Moodera, who made the 1995 discovery, so any trio misrepresents something. This is the reason I no longer prefer B037. On B007 I agree with him that the omitted HgTe-proposal and 3D contributors and the 2016 prize make it an alternative, not a first choice, and I keep it as my second alternative on those terms.

uncertainties: Whether a two-name credit for Katori and Ye can be defended against the first-demonstration claims of Takamoto and Ido and the contributions of Lemonde, and whether the citation wording does enough to confine Ye's credit to the lattice clock.

Whether the committee regards the many-atom, light-shift-cancelled lattice as a principle beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge that it is, but that is a judgement and Pearce is entitled to disagree.

Whether I have moved because of the physics or because my own preference could not be placed in three names; I believe the second, which is a legitimate reason, but it means the scientific case for B037 was not tested against the clock case on equal terms.
Whether the committee will want a second look at B037 in a later year as a prize for the MgO step with Parkin and Yuasa, with the 2007 prize as background.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. B037 lies close to my field of theoretical magnetism, but I have no documented connection to Moodera, Parkin or Miyazaki, and I no longer prefer it. I have no documented connection to Katori or Ye; B042 is outside my own field. My co-authors and collaborators in the profile are not among the credited names for any shortlisted ballot.
